attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, not a quote of anyone else.

semantics.note: Keeps 'vast majority', 'meaningful revenue', 'if they've turned them on at all' and the warehouse majority. Correctly drops the normative point about what NVIDIA should disclose. Firm present-tense assertion.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary: count companies, measure real revenue from the GPUs, and treat 'most' as more than half of sold hardware sitting in storage. Using Q2 2026 as the latest common quarter is a reasonable choice for an ongoing state.

evidence.note: Telemetry from an installed fleet of 342k accelerators, measured in GPU-hours. It cannot measure hardware that never reached a cluster, or how many buyers earn real revenue.
Microsoft's own disclosure of total cloud revenue for the quarter. One company, and a broader measure than revenue from GPUs; it does not cover the whole buyer population.

reviews.rationale: Neither item measures what the contract requires: a representative census of buyers' GPU revenue, or records linking shipments to deployment that show how much hardware sits in warehouses. The utilization study covers installed hardware only. Microsoft's figure is one company's broad cloud revenue. Neither majority claim can be confirmed or refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I don't see how ... ever' is strong disbelief, not a probability hedge, so it reads as a firm forecast with no deadline. The investor-protection part keeps its condition (if demand never arrives).

contract.note: Reading 'revenue' as money buyers earn from the hardware, not profit, is ordinary. Weighting by sales value and using hardware sold by publication are evaluator choices that the contract discloses, and it also asks for unit-weighted results. Leaving the conditional part unscored is correct.

evidence.note: NVIDIA's own claim, on its own earnings call, that its compute is fully utilized. A company disclosure about utilization, not matched records of buyers' revenue, so it cannot test the 10% threshold.
Law-firm analysis showing one backstop that applies only under conditions. It does not measure protection across the sector, and the demand-failure condition has not occurred.

reviews.rationale: The forecast covers the whole life of the hardware and has no deadline. The early-contradiction rule needs matched records showing more than 10% of a defined sales cohort has already earned revenue; the packet has none, only NVIDIA's own utilization claim. The investor-protection part is conditional, and its condition has not occurred. Not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the universal denial and the hardball exception. It drops 'or reason for', a minor narrowing that does not change what is tested. A firm present-tense claim about procurement economics.

contract.note: The result depends on whether supply-certainty benefits count as independent of vendor pressure, and whether 'buying' means reserving or taking delivery. The speaker defined neither. The contract flags both and excludes benefits caused only by vendor pressure, which is fair.

evidence.note: Expert analysis saying advance commitments buy certainty of supply. That certainty comes from allocation by distributors and vendors, so it is not shown to be independent of vendor pressure, and it concerns reservations, not stored hardware.
A supplier's blog: hardware that arrives before the site is ready sits idle. Consistent with the claim that early delivery has no benefit, but it does not show that no independent advantage exists.

reviews.rationale: The contract would count a single well-documented counterexample: an advantage from buying early that does not depend on NVIDIA's pressure. The packet has none. The supply-certainty benefit comes from vendor and distributor allocation. Nothing shows the universal claim holds either. Not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: 'I believe' is not a graded hedge, and 'inevitable' commits him to the outcome, so it is a forecast with no deadline. It keeps the point that there will be no tidy dot-com-style exit.

contract.note: Defining overbuild as sustained, material excess capacity that paying demand cannot support, with losses, is the ordinary reading and matches the surrounding text. Correctly sets no deadline and requires an industry-scale episode before early resolution.

evidence.note: CBRE's H1 2026 leasing vacancy of 1.4% in major North American markets. Today's tight conditions cannot refute a forecast with no deadline, and the figure does not measure GPU workload utilization.
October 2026 log of posted GPU rental prices, mostly rising. A snapshot of list prices, not realized utilization or eventual economics, and not an episode that meets the resolution rule.

reviews.rationale: No deadline, and no industry-wide episode of excess capacity driven by weak demand, with unrecovered losses, is documented by the cutoff. The current tightness in leasing and rental prices cannot refute a forecast with no deadline. Not settled.
